## Overview

Pupil size changes slowly after an experimental event, often producing a response whose magnitude and latency depend on task demands. In this tutorial, we use `neurogam` to address a time-resolved question: **when does pupil size differ between easy and difficult arithmetic problems?**

The workflow is:

1. Import a small, publicly available pupillometry dataset.
2. Briefly preprocess the recordings and inspect data quality.
3. Summarise repeated trials within participants, conditions, and time bins.
4. Fit a Bayesian generalised additive multilevel model (BGAMM).
5. Inspect posterior time courses, evidence thresholds, and model diagnostics.

**Scope.** This is a worked example of `neurogam`, not a general preprocessing
standard. The original sample has nine participants; one is excluded for poor
data quality, leaving approximately eight participants before any further
exclusions. Consequently, the analysis is illustrative.

## Dataset and experimental contrast

The `pupil_data` dataset from
[`PupillometryR`](https://samhforbes.github.io/PupillometryR/) comes from a
demonstration study of easy and difficult arithmetic problems. Each observation
contains the participant, trial, condition, elapsed time in milliseconds, and
pupil measurements for the left and right eye. The dataset is installed with
the package; no manual download is required.

## Import and preprocess

We follow the basic operations described in the `PupillometryR` tutorial:
mark invalid samples, combine the two eyes, downsample to 50-ms bins, remove
trials with substantial missingness, filter, interpolate short gaps, and
subtract a trial-specific baseline.

```{r data-import}
library(PupillometryR)
library(neurogam)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# use the ggplot2 neurogam theme
theme_set(theme_neurogam() )

# import the pupil data
# see https://samhforbes.github.io/PupillometryR/articles/PupillometryR.html
data("pupil_data")

# check that IDs are not numeric
pupil_data$ID <- as.character(pupil_data$ID)

# remove participant number 8, who had problematic data
pupil_data <- subset(pupil_data, ID != 8)

# blinks were registered as -1, so replace with NAs
pupil_data$LPupil[pupil_data$LPupil == -1] <- NA
pupil_data$RPupil[pupil_data$RPupil == -1] <- NA

# reshape the data
Sdata <- make_pupillometryr_data(
    data = pupil_data,
    subject = ID,
    trial = Trial,
    time = Time,
    condition = Type
    )

new_data <- replace_missing_data(data = Sdata)
regressed_data <- regress_data(data = new_data, pupil1 = RPupil, pupil2 = LPupil)

mean_data <- calculate_mean_pupil_size(
    data = regressed_data,
    pupil1 = RPupil,
    pupil2 = LPupil
    )

mean_data <- downsample_time_data(
    data = mean_data,
    pupil = mean_pupil,
    timebin_size = 50,
    option = "median"
    )

missing <- calculate_missing_data(mean_data,  mean_pupil)

mean_data2 <- clean_missing_data(
    mean_data,
    pupil = mean_pupil,
    trial_threshold = 0.75,
    subject_trial_threshold = 0.75
    )

filtered_data <- filter_data(
    data = mean_data2,
    pupil = mean_pupil,
    filter = "median",
    degree = 11
    )

int_data <- interpolate_data(
    data = filtered_data,
    pupil = mean_pupil,
    type = "linear"
    )

base_data <- baseline_data(
    data = int_data,
    pupil = mean_pupil,
    start = 0,
    stop = 100
    )
```

## Explore the observed responses

Visualise participant-average trajectories first, before inspecting the grand
mean. This reveals the large variability that is otherwise hidden by a single
group-level summary.

```{r observed-participants, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 12}
base_data %>%
     # average trials within each participant
    group_by(ID, Type, Time) %>%
    summarise(
        mean_pupil = mean(mean_pupil, na.rm = TRUE),
        .groups = "drop"
        ) %>%
    # group-level mean and SEM across participants
    group_by(Type, Time) %>%
    summarise(
        mean = mean(mean_pupil, na.rm = TRUE),
        sem = sd(mean_pupil, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(mean_pupil) ) ),
        .groups = "drop"
        ) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = Time, y = mean, fill = Type, colour = Type) ) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) +
    geom_ribbon(
        aes(
            ymin = mean - sem,
            ymax = mean + sem
            ),
        alpha = 0.25,
        colour = NA
        ) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    labs(
        x = "Time (ms)",
        y = "Mean pupil response",
        colour = "Condition",
        fill = "Condition"
        )
```

## Fit the Bayesian GAMM

We estimate a smooth response for each condition together with participant variation. `kvalue` controls the maximum flexibility of the smooth terms, not the number of temporal clusters. Fitting may take several minutes or longer depending on the hardware and Stan backend.

**Baseline caveat.** This dataset begins after event onset, so 0-100 ms is not
a true pre-event baseline. A pre-stimulus baseline would normally be preferable
when available. An apparent difference emerging immediately after event onset
should also be considered with particular caution given the latency of the
pupillary response.

```{r clusters, results = "hide"}
# centering and scaling predictors
base_data <- data.frame(base_data)
base_data$Type <- as.factor(base_data$Type)
contrasts(base_data$Type) <- c(-0.5, 0.5)
base_data <- base_data %>% select(-Trial, -Timebin)

# load cached results
previous_results <- readRDS(file = "cache/pupillometry_results.rds")
reuse_model <- previous_results$model

# fit the BGAMM to identify clusters
results <- testing_through_time(
    # pupillometry data
    data = base_data,
    # reuse a previous model
    previous_model = reuse_model,
    # participant column
    participant_id = "ID",
    # outcome column
    outcome_id = "mean_pupil",
    # name of predictor in data
    predictor_id = "Type",
    # time column
    time_id = "Time",
    # time_id = "Time_scaled",
    # basis dimension
    # kvalue = 30,
    kvalue = 20,
    # we recommend fitting the model on summary statistics (mean and SEM)
    multilevel = "summary",
    # include an AR(1) autocorrelation structure
    # include_ar_term = TRUE,
    # threshold on posterior odds
    threshold = 2,
    # number of MCMCs
    chains = 4,
    # number of parallel cores
    cores = 4,
    # list of Stan control arguments
    stan_control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95, max_treedepth = 12),
    # define the baseline window (used to compute the ROPE)
    baseline_window = c(0, 100)
    )

# check the model formula
results$model$formula

# save the results
# saveRDS(object = results, file = "cache/pupillometry_results.rds")
```

## Inspect the posterior and temporal clusters

Inspect the full posterior trajectory rather than reporting only the detected
clusters. In particular, check whether the posterior difference is stable
across adjacent times, whether its amplitude is scientifically relevant, and
whether any cluster depends strongly on the threshold or spline flexibility.

```{r print-clusters}
# visualise the identified clusters
print(results)
```

```{r plot-clusters}
# visualise the data, model's predictions, and clusters
plot(results)
```

## Model diagnostics

Start by examining the fitted model for sampling problems such as divergent
transitions, low effective sample size, and large $\hat R$ values.

```{r model-summary}
summary(results$model)
```

Next, compare fitted values with participant trajectories. The convenience
`ppc()` method provided by `neurogam` is useful, but inspect residual
structure and any remaining temporal autocorrelation as well.

```{r posterior-checks}
neurogam::ppc(object = results, ppc_type = "group")
neurogam::ppc(object = results, ppc_type = "participant")
```
